articleSummary: Two hantavirus groups drive disease: Old World (Eurasia, including Russia) causes hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS); New World (Americas) causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS). The outbreak affects kuroiler, broiler, layer, and local chicken and duck varieties. Infected birds show flu-like signs, including head swelling, nasal discharge, and sudden death. The disease is widespread in Imphal East across Khurai, Keirao, Thongju, Bamon Kampu, Kongba, Wangkhei, Akampat, and Kongpal, with Imphal West reporting cases in Ningombam, Langol, Iroishemba, Lamshang, Samurou, and Yumnam Huidrom. A Thongju Ningomthong grower reported 30 egg-laying hens dying suddenly before veterinary consultation. Some farmers are underselling infected or potentially exposed birds, with prices reportedly as low as Rs 200 per head for large 3–4 kg birds. Farmers allege the Veterinary and Animal Husbandry Department has not yet collected samples. They urge immediate testing and intervention to curb the outbreak and reduce economic losses.

articleSummary: As of 2026-05-16, Iran has no reported hantavirus cases and the outbreak risk is very low, with adherence to environmental hygiene to prevent potential infections. Hantavirus is a rodent-borne zoonosis; humans typically become infected via inhalation of dust contaminated with rodent saliva, urine, or feces, or contact with contaminated materials. Human-to-human transmission is rare and unlikely to cause a pandemic. articleSummary: 65 died in northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo from Ebola; authorities confirmed 13 cases in Kinshasa; over 200 suspected, with four deaths in Ituri confirmed as Ebola. articleSummary: Hantavirus natural foci in Russia cover the Far East (Primorsky Krai), European part, Krasnodar Krai, Ural, and Western Siberia, according to infectious-disease clinician Yulia Ermolaeva of Novosibirsk State University. She lists Primorsky Krai, the Far East, European Russia, Krasnodar Krai, Ural, and Western Siberia as major natural foci where infected rodents harbor the virus. The 2026 cruise-ship outbreak and reports of the infection being imported to Thailand from South America show global hantavirus circulation, with travelers potentially facing different pathogen serotypes. Hantavirus infection is described as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and a natural focal disease tied to landscapes inhabited by infected rodents. In Russia, main vectors are voles and mice, per Academician Gennady Onishchenko; the virus persists in certain animal hosts. Vaccine development is projected to take ~1.5 years, and experts question whether Atlantic hemorrhagic fever outbreaks could spark a pandemic.

articleSummary: Measles reemerges in Latin America amid a vaccination crisis driven by waning confidence, misinformation, and unequal access. In Q1 2026, regional measles cases exceed 15,300 (OPS), surpassing 2025's 14,975 across 13 countries; the Americas accounted for 21% of global cases in the first three months of 2026. Colombia reported six imported cases; Mexico registered the highest number of reports at 740. The region, once certified measles-free in 2016, lost that status in 2018, regained in 2024, lost again in 2025, and is slumping in 2026. articleHeadline: Early Symptoms vs Warning Signs: When Does Dengue Become Life-Threatening? Doctor Answers
articleSummary: Dengue, spread by Aedes mosquitoes, begins with high fever, body aches, headache, pain behind the eyes, nausea, vomiting and rash—symptoms often mistaken for a viral illness. In India’s monsoon and post-monsoon season, most patients recover with rest and fluids, but warning signs must not be ignored. The critical phase typically occurs between days 4 and 7, when fever may subside but blood vessels can leak and platelets fall, risking hypotension and organ dysfunction. Urgent care is needed for warning signs such as persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, confusion, bleeding (gum, nose, vomit, or black stools), or breathlessness. Severe dengue can progress to Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever or Dengue Shock Syndrome, requiring hospital care, intravenous fluids, and sometimes intensive care. Early recognition and careful fluid management improve outcomes.

articleSummary: On National Dengue Day (May 16), Mumbai-based infectious-disease specialist Dr Amol Jaybhaye warns dengue can be far more dangerous than a typical fever. Dengue, spread by Aedes mosquitoes, may start with fever and body pain but can rapidly worsen to dehydration, breathing trouble, liver complications, bleeding, and a sudden drop in platelets, potentially causing shock—especially in children, the elderly, pregnant women, or those with existing conditions. Warning signs include repeated vomiting, inability to eat, stomach pain, extreme weakness, bleeding gums, and breathing difficulty; delayed treatment and self-medication worsen outcomes. Treatment emphasizes hydration, regular monitoring, and symptom relief, with no specific cure. Prevention matters most: eliminate standing water in coolers, flower pots, buckets, terraces, and other containers; wear protective clothing, use repellents, and maintain clean surroundings, particularly during the monsoon peak (June–November).

articleSummary: Dengue fever, a mosquito-borne viral illness transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, typically begins with fever and flu-like symptoms during the monsoon season in India. Initial signs include high fever, body pains, headache, weakness, retro-orbital pain, chills, and sometimes rash. Most patients recover with rest, fluids, and timely medical care, but ignoring symptoms heightens risk. Symptoms resemble a common viral infection; a rapid escalation can occur as the illness progresses. A critical phase usually develops between days 4 and 7, with possible drops in blood pressure and organ function and falling platelets. While low platelets do not always indicate severe dengue, a rapid decline with worsening symptoms signals danger. Some patients may have confusion, bleeding from gums or nose, vomiting blood, dark stools, or fluid buildup in chest or abdomen, causing breathlessness and requiring urgent care. The article cites guidance from Gurugram's Fortis Memorial Research Institute and stresses hydration and avoiding self-treatment.

articleHeadline: A guide to testing for sexually transmitted infections
articleSummary: India is experiencing a sharp rise in common sexually transmitted infections (STIs), with an estimated 30 million infections annually (5-6% of adults). Syphilis incidence is about 3 cases per 1,000 person-years in certain populations, and gonorrhoea prevalence is increasing among adolescents and young adults. Antimicrobial resistance is rising, including drug‑resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae, signaling a potential STI epidemic if surveillance and control are not strengthened. Many STIs are asymptomatic; HIV, HPV, and HCV can be silent, while symptoms—when present—often include genital discharge (gonorrhoea: yellow discharge; other infections with foul-smelling or curdy discharge) or ulcers (syphilis: painless ulcers; herpes: painful blisters). Testing is essential during pregnancy and for those with unprotected sex, new or unknown partners, or multiple partners. However, testing is gendered, with women facing stigma and access barriers. Because infections have different incubation periods, testing should occur when appropriate: at least four weeks post-exposure, then at three months; post-exposure prophylaxis is discussed for immediate exposure.

articleSummary: Transmission of Hantavirus occurs via two routes: animal-borne and, rarely, human-to-human. The main route is from rodent carriers—primarily rats and shrews—through bites or exposure to urine, feces, saliva, or dust contaminated with viral secretions. At-risk groups include sanitation workers, farmers, construction workers, pest controllers, sewer workers, and laboratory personnel handling rodent hosts; outdoor activities such as camping increase exposure risk. By contrast, Hantavirus type HFRS (hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome) is found in Asia, Europe, and Indonesia, with no evidence of human-to-human spread. In Indonesia, reported cases have been Seoul type causing HFRS, not HPS.

articleSummary: As of May 16, 2026, the Democratic Republic of Congo reports 246 suspected Ebola virus disease cases and 80 deaths. The first suspected case was a nurse who died after fever, bleeding, vomiting and severe weakness, treated at the Evangelical Medical Center in Bunia. The government activated the national health emergency operations center, strengthened epidemiologic and laboratory surveillance, and mobilized rapid-response teams. Africa CDC is convening an emergency meeting with Congo, Uganda, South Sudan and international partners to bolster cross-border surveillance, preparedness, and intervention. Lab results indicate a strain different from the Zaire lineage, with sequencing underway. Virologist Jean-Jacques Muyembe notes that all but one of Congo’s 16 prior outbreaks were due to the Zaire strain; a non-Zaire variant could complicate treatments and vaccines developed against Zaire. Given high cross-border movement, rapid regional coordination is essential, says Africa CDC Director Jean Kaseya.
notes: 新型エボラ株（非Zaire系統）の出現により、既存ワクチン・治療法の効果が低下する可能性があり、極めて懸念が高い。ウガンダ・南スーダンとの国境監視強化が急務。Africa CDCによる緊急会議召集により国際的対応が既に進行中。

articleSummary: Bundibugyo ebolavirus strain outbreak in Ituri, northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo, near the Ugandan border, with about 246 suspected cases and at least 65 deaths. Some cases are laboratory-confirmed, and transmission may have continued for weeks. There are no approved vaccines or specific treatments for Bundibugyo; clinicians may use experimental antivirals with limited efficacy. WHO has deployed epidemiologists, laboratory experts, and PPE to the region, with ongoing delivery of equipment and test systems. The outbreak is concentrated in hard-to-reach areas where weak infrastructure, conflict, and population movement around mining settlements could accelerate spread. Ebola can be highly lethal, with case fatality up to 90% depending on access to care. Unlike the Zaïre strain, vaccines for Bundibugyo are in early development; the risk of global spread remains low, and no sustained transmission outside Africa has been documented.

articleHeadline: At least 65 killed as rare strain of Ebola with no approved vaccines spreads in Congo
articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (Ituri) has killed at least 65 people. Laboratory confirmation shifted from an initial negative test for Ebola Zaire to Bundibugyo on May 14; the presumed first case was a nurse who died April 24 at the Evangelical Medical Center in Bunia. A Congolese patient infected across the border in Uganda died in Kampala on May 14, with the body repatriated to Congo that evening. Symptoms include fever, weakness, vomiting and bleeding; transmission is via direct contact with bodily fluids, intensified by poor sanitation and crowded mining settlements. No approved vaccines or widely deployed countermeasures exist for Bundibugyo; remdesivir is considered. WHO is deploying epidemiologists, lab specialists and infection-control experts, and airlifting five metric tons of supplies. The outbreak is about 1,700 km from Kinshasa, in a fragile region; the US warns against travel to Ituri. Imported/exported cases have been limited.

articleSummary: Patna, India faces rising dengue risk as temperatures climb and monsoon nears (expected second week of June). Despite about 1,600 dengue cases in 2025, pre-monsoon anti-larva spray and fogging campaigns are progressing slowly. Reported mosquito activity is high in areas such as Kankarbagh, Rajiv Nagar, Patna City, Gardniabagh, Boring Road, Ashiana, Danapur and Phulwari Sharif, with day-time biting now common. Water-logging hotspots—Kankarbagh, Rajendra Nagar, Patliputra, New Bypass and other low-lying zones—remain particularly vulnerable due to open drains and stagnant water. Historical counts: 2022 7,605; 2023 8,493; 2024 5,041; 2025 Sep 354, Nov 1,640; 2026 early 48. Health authorities fear post-monsoon spikes if May-end campaigns are not intensified; schools will run dengue awareness from July. Preventive steps include eliminating standing water, cleaning tanks and coolers, wearing full-sleeve clothing, using nets and repellents, and seeking prompt medical care for fever, headache and body pains.
notes: 2025年に約1,600件のデング熱症例が報告されており、過去数年の流行データ（2022年7,605件、2023年8,493件）と比較して増加傾向。モンスーン期（6月第2週予想）に向けた重要な時期にあり、蚊の活動が高く、水溜まりが多い地区での流行拡大リスクが高い。健康当局が対策の強化を警告しており、学校でもデング熱啓発活動を予定している。

articleSummary: Eight suspected hantavirus cases aboard a cruise bound for Cabo Verde are reported as of May 15, highlighting five rat-borne zoonoses. Murine typhus (Rickettsia typhi/mooseri) via rat fleas; fever, headache, rash. Salmonellosis (Salmonella) from contaminated food/water; diarrhea, fever, vomiting; dehydration; severe cases may need antibiotics. Andes hantavirus transmission human-to-human is rare and not recorded in Brazil.

Cases cluster in Bunia, Mongbwalu, and Rwampara, where mining-driven population movement and security challenges hinder containment; no approved vaccine exists for Bundibugyo. Four of the confirmed cases have died, and the outbreak marks the 17th Ebola outbreak in DRC since 1976. The DRC has activated its Public Health Emergency Operations Center and boosted surveillance and lab capacity; WHO and MSF have dispatched teams to assess risk and aid containment. In neighboring Uganda, a 59-year-old man who had traveled from DRC died in Kampala. Ebola spreads via direct contact with infected fluids; Bundibugyo’s mortality is about 37%, lower than the Ebola Zaire strain’s ~90%. Origins believed to involve bats.

articleSummary: Ebola virus (Zaire ebolavirus) is at the center of a new outbreak in DR Congo, with a death reported in Uganda; the disease has caused over 15,000 deaths in Africa across five decades. Bats are the natural reservoir; other mammals can transmit to humans. Human-to-human transmission occurs via direct contact with bodily fluids; funeral rites amplify spread. Age risk skews: 65% of deaths occur in those over 65; 45–64 account for ~23%. Southeast Asia (Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, Philippines, Malaysia) was most affected regionally, while Americas show the sharpest life-expectancy declines. articleHeadline: No vaccine for latest Ebola outbreak, DRC warns as as toll hits 80
articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak detected in Ituri province, northeastern DRC, near Uganda and South Sudan. As of 2026-05-16, 246 suspected cases and 80 deaths reported; Uganda records one cross-border death of a DRC national in Kampala, with tests confirming Bundibugyo strain (first identified in 2007). No vaccine or specific treatment exists for Bundibugyo; vaccines are available only for the Zaire strain (identified in 1976) with a 60-90% fatality rate. Bundibugyo can have about 50% lethality. Patient zero was a nurse who presented in Bunia on April 24 with fever, haemorrhaging, and vomiting. Transmission occurs via contact with bodily fluids from symptomatic patients; incubation up to 21 days. WHO is airlifting five tonnes of infection-prevention gear, highlighting cross-border spread risk due to population movements. Previous DRC Ebola outbreaks include August last year (at least 34 deaths) and a 2018–2020 episode with ~2,300 deaths.

An imported case in Uganda involves a 59-year-old Congolese man hospitalized May 11 who died May 14; Ugandan authorities consider it imported from DRC with no locally confirmed case yet. Africa CDC notes provisional figures pending laboratory confirmation, line-list harmonization, contact tracing and epidemiological investigation. The agency is coordinating a rapid regional response with DRC, Uganda, South Sudan and partners to interrupt transmission, protect communities, and reduce cross-border spread. articleSummary: Minas Gerais, Brazil, confirmed a February hantavirus death on 11 May, three months after the death, highlighting hantavirus as an endemic threat in Brazil for over three decades with late diagnoses. The confirmed-case fatality is about 46.5%, suggesting real mortality is higher due to underdiagnosis. The episode coincides with an international alert after eight people fell ill and three died aboard the MV Hondius, a voyage from Ushuaia to Antarctica, linked to Andes hantavirus with rare human-to-human transmission. In Brazil, hantavirus is endemic; the first Brazilian case was in 1993 (Juquitiba, São Paulo). From 2013-2023, over 13,000 suspected cases were reported, 758 confirmed, about 40% fatal. Brazilian variants include Araraquara (Cerrado, aggressive), Juquitiba, Castelo dos Sonhos, Anajatuba, Laguna Negra, Paranoá, Rio Mamoré. Transmission is via inhalation of dried rodent excreta; incubation 1-8 weeks; symptoms start like flu and can progress to severe cardiopulmonary failure; no specific antiviral; vaccines do not cover American variants; treatment is supportive.

articleSummary: 246 suspected Ebola cases and 80 deaths have been reported in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), while Uganda recorded one death in Kampala from a Congolese national; no confirmed cases in Uganda. This marks the DRC’s 17th Ebola outbreak. The Bundibugyo ebolavirus strain is involved, with mortality potentially up to 50%, and there is no vaccine or specific treatment. Testing has been conducted only in Kinshasa; numerous suspected cases suggest rapid spread. The epicenter is Ituri province in northeast DRC, bordering Uganda and South Sudan, a mining region with cross-border movement. The zero patient was a nurse who presented April 24 in Bunia with fever, bleeding and vomiting. Access to parts of Ituri is hindered by armed groups and poor roads. The previous DRC outbreak (Aug–Dec 2025) was contained. Ebola remains deadly; transmission occurs via bodily fluids after symptom onset, with incubation up to 21 days.

articleSummary: As of May 16, 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo reports an Ebola outbreak in Ituri Province caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus. The strain, previously detected in Uganda and in Isiro, Haut-Uele, in 2012, was confirmed after samples arrived at INRB Kinshasa on May 13 and were validated on May 14. Initial testing for Zaire ebolavirus was negative; Bundibugyo confirmation followed. Authorities are conducting active case finding and contact tracing, including identification of deaths in the community. Bundibugyo ebolavirus, first identified in 2007 in Uganda’s Bundibugyo District, causes severe hemorrhagic fever with a maculopapular rash, vascular damage, coagulation disturbances, and potential multi-organ failure. The outbreak unfolds amid violence by ADF and local militias (CODECO, Zaïre, CRP), triggering displacement. It follows the December 1, 2025 declaration of the end of DRC’s 16th Ebola outbreak in Kasaï (last discharge Oct 19, 2025; 42 days with no new cases).

articleSummary: Dengue now frequently presents with gastrointestinal symptoms—nausea, abdominal pain, bloating, vomiting, and reduced appetite—often before classic fever and body pain. Liver involvement is common, with elevated enzymes and fatigue; in severe cases, liver injury can progress to liver failure, with higher risk for those with fatty liver, chronic liver disease, diabetes, obesity, or alcohol-related liver conditions. Management emphasizes hydration, monitoring blood pressure, liver function, urine output, and signs of plasma leakage beyond platelet counts.
